summary:
Madre de Dios has no distinct trans-specific law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement record in the material reviewed for this dossier; the national framework therefore governs what a trans visitor to the department faces. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, removed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women continues to rise.

Restroom access is restricted nationally. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously a merged dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante of Honor y Democracia, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The text lists narrow exceptions for custody, required medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bill followed a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the text and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same requirement into force for trans people, including trans youth, and the legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Enforcement is expected to rest on the judgement of individual security staff. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that access to restrooms would depend on staff discretion, including checks of identity documents, and notes that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television the presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV told Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, to 'go use the men's room'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that the restroom provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute states that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, and cites UN reporting showing that trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru for 2020-2023, with trans women accounting for more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020. A 2024 report on rising hate crimes found trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stated that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One case sets a legal precedent for the region. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
